**b)** Find the exact numerical value that lies exactly halfway between 10 and 100 on a logarithmic scale. Contrast this with the arithmetic midpoint on a linear scale.

<div data-log="midpoint" class="log-demo"></div>

::: {.column-block}

**c)** A scientist is measuring the masses of various cells and viruses ranging from $10^{-6}$ g to $10^6$ g. Justify why a logarithmic scale is more appropriate than a linear scale for plotting these masses.

::: {.log-hint}
**Hint:** Compare the exponents at the two ends of the range.
:::

:::
::::

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 40 · Example 3.1(b–c)</p>

::: notes

Work the midpoint in OneNote before using Show midpoints. A midpoint on the logarithmic axis has log10(x)=(1+2)/2=3/2, so x=10^(3/2)=10√10=√1000≈31.6227766. Its ratio to 10 equals the ratio of 100 to it: √10. The linear midpoint is (10+100)/2=55. The two diagrams use equal physical lengths, with separate labels for their scales. Reset hides both midpoint values.

For (c), retain the supplied hypothetical range. It spans 12 orders of magnitude, with largest-to-smallest ratio 10^12. A linear scale large enough for 10^6 g crowds small masses near zero; a logarithmic scale allocates equal space to equal ratios and makes relative comparisons readable. All masses are positive. Allow about 5 minutes.

:::
